issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of an entire parcel is not excessive or a colourable exercise of power when the parcel is required for the facilities of an integrated public town-planning scheme.
material_facts: The acquired parcel was intended for a road, a walking platform and a service platform along a river, as well as a neighbourhood centre, public garden and playground under a town-planning scheme.
The acquiring corporation’s affidavit explained the planned facilities and how they required the whole parcel.
The High Court accepted those factual averments, and the Supreme Court treated its findings as incontrovertible.
issues.conclusion: The contention that the whole parcel was unnecessary, and the related contention that the acquisition exceeded the requirements, were rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Whether the whole parcel is required is assessed against the public purpose and the actual facilities contemplated by the scheme. The accepted factual findings showed that the parcel was required for the scheme’s several facilities; the judgment cites no earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding challenges the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.scheme_includes_multiple_public_faciliti: The acquiring authority’s scheme provides for several public facilities on or along the land.
predicates.evidence_shows_entire_parcel_needed: Evidence accepted by the court shows that the whole parcel is needed for the facilities contemplated by the scheme.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a land acquisition and accepted evidence shows that the whole parcel is needed for a scheme’s multiple public facilities, the acquisition is not excessive.

issues.legal_issue: A notification declaring a public purpose is not invalid merely because it does not identify the instrumentality that will carry out that purpose.
material_facts: The challenge to the acquisition notifications asserted that the declaration of public purpose was invalid because it did not identify the instrumentality through which the purpose would be carried out.
The Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court had held that omission of the instrumentality did not invalidate a notification, and the Supreme Court had confirmed that view.
issues.conclusion: The omission of the instrumentality from the notification did not invalidate it, and the contention was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, failure to specify the instrumentality that will execute the public purpose does not affect the validity of the notification. The Court relied on Ramji Popatbhai Patel v. Jamnadas Shah, Kanaiyalal Maneklal Chinai v. State of Gujarat, and Vishnu Prasad Ramdas Gohil v. State of Gujarat.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a notification for acquiring land.
predicates.notification_states_public_purpose: The notification identifies the public purpose for which the land is acquired.
predicates.notification_omits_executing_instrumenta: The notification does not identify the body or agency that will carry out the public purpose.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition notification states its public purpose but omits the body that will carry it out, the notification remains valid.
